coverage: All named people and identifiable divine references in both English editions, including Caesar as a title rather than an invented individual. Hypothetical examples excluded.

entities.name: Socrates
entities.body: The Athenian philosopher, used as an example of living by reason.

entities.name: Diogenes
entities.body: Diogenes of Sinope, the Cynic philosopher known for rejecting conventional comforts.

entities.name: Heraclitus
entities.body: The Greek philosopher from Ephesus, cited alongside Diogenes.

entities.name: Euphrates
entities.body: A philosopher from Syria admired for his eloquent teaching.

entities.name: Caesar
entities.body: A title for the Roman emperor; this example does not identify a particular ruler.

entities.name: Polynices
entities.body: Eteocles’ brother, one of the rival sons of Oedipus in Greek legend.

entities.name: Eteocles
entities.body: Polynices’ brother, one of the rival sons of Oedipus in Greek legend.

entities.name: Apollo
entities.body: The Greek god whose oracle speaks at Delphi.

entities.name: Zeno
entities.body: Zeno of Citium, the founder of the Stoic school of philosophy.

entities.name: Chrysippus
entities.body: An early Stoic philosopher whose writings helped develop the school’s teachings.

entities.name: Homer
entities.body: The Greek poet traditionally credited with the Iliad and Odyssey.

entities.name: Zeus
entities.body: The chief Greek god, invoked in the closing verses.

entities.name: Destiny
entities.body: Fate addressed as a guiding power in the closing verses.

entities.name: Crito
entities.body: Socrates’ friend, addressed in the quotation from Plato’s Crito.

entities.name: Anytus
entities.body: One of Socrates’ accusers at his trial in Athens.

entities.name: Melitus / Meletus
entities.body: One of Socrates’ accusers at his trial in Athens.
